Key takeaways
  • While the Squid Game craze has settled, dalgona candy is still available in Seoul, often for tourists or as a nostalgic treat.
  • You can find dalgona from street vendors in popular tourist areas like Myeongdong and Insadong, or at some traditional markets.
  • For a modern twist, look for dalgona-flavored items in cafes or buy DIY kits at large marts for the authentic challenge.
👤 This is for readers who are curious about the current status of dalgona candy in Korea, want to know where to buy it, or are considering making it themselves.

You’ve probably seen the buzz online about dalgona candy (달고나), especially after Squid Game exploded. For foreigners wondering where to buy dalgona candy in Seoul right now, in August 2026, the short answer is: it’s around, but it’s not quite the phenomenon it once was. It’s more of a nostalgic treat or a tourist experience these days, rather than something every Korean is lining up for.

Is Dalgona Candy Still a Major Trend in Korea (as of 2026)?

Honestly, no, not like it was during the peak of Squid Game. When the show first aired, dalgona (the sugary brittle candy, also known as ppoppop (뽑뽑) in its original street food form) was everywhere. Street vendors popped up overnight, cafes launched dalgona lattes, and people were furiously trying to cut out shapes with toothpicks. It was a proper craze. Now, in 2026, the initial hype has definitely cooled off among locals. It’s become a bit like a seasonal hit song – everyone knew it, loved it for a bit, and now it plays occasionally on a retro playlist. In my office, someone still brings in a dalgona-flavored snack once in a while, usually for a laugh or to reminisce, but nobody’s doing the actual challenge anymore. It’s primarily a nostalgic item for Koreans, and a curiosity for tourists still connecting it to the show.

Point: It's a fun memento or a sweet trip down memory lane, not the current hottest thing.

Where to Buy Dalgona Candy from Street Vendors & Traditional Markets

If you're looking for that authentic, street-side dalgona candy Squid Game experience, your best bet for where to buy it is still in the major tourist hubs. Areas like Myeongdong (명동), Insadong (인사동), and parts of Hongdae (홍대) still have a handful of dedicated street vendors. These vendors often have the full setup: the portable burner, the ladle, the presses, and the array of shapes. They’re usually catering specifically to tourists, complete with photo opportunities. I remember walking through Myeongdong recently after a late hoesik (the after-work company dinner) and seeing a line of foreign visitors excitedly trying to choose their shape, even though it was almost midnight. The price for a piece of dalgona from a street vendor typically ranges from 2,000 to 5,000 won (roughly $1.50-$4 USD), depending on the size and complexity of the shape. You might also find a vendor or two in larger traditional markets, like Gwangjang Market (광장시장), though they're less common than during the peak.

Point: Tourist hotspots are your best bet for the classic street vendor experience, but be prepared for a slightly higher price.

Modern Dalgona Twists: Cafes, Convenience Stores, and Souvenirs

Beyond the street, dalgona has integrated itself into the modern Korean snack landscape in more subtle ways. Many cafes still offer dalgona lattes or dalgona-flavored desserts, where the crunchy, burnt-sugar flavor is incorporated into a drink or topping, rather than being a standalone candy you break. These are pretty common and can be a nice way to enjoy the taste without the pressure of the challenge. The first time I tried a dalgona latte, I was surprised by how well the bitter-sweet crunch complemented the coffee. For those wondering where to buy dalgona candy for convenience, some larger convenience stores (편의점, pyeon-ui-jeom) like GS25 or CU occasionally stock pre-packaged dalgona-flavored snacks or actual small pieces of the candy, especially around popular seasons or as a limited-edition item. You won't find it year-round everywhere, but it pops up. Additionally, you can find souvenir-style dalgona kits in large supermarkets (마트, mateu) like E-Mart or Lotte Mart, or in souvenir shops in tourist areas. These kits typically include the small ladle, a press, and the specific metal shapes, allowing you to try making it yourself at home.

Point: Cafes offer the flavor without the fuss; kits are great for DIY fun; convenience stores are hit-or-miss for pre-made candy.

Making Your Own Dalgona: The True Squid Game Challenge

For many, the real fun of dalgona candy, especially in the context of Squid Game, isn't just eating it but trying to carve out the shape without it breaking. This is where making your own comes in. Honestly, this is probably the most rewarding way to experience it now, as it truly brings the show's challenge to life. My coworker recently bought a DIY kit for his kid, and they spent an entire Saturday afternoon laughing and screaming as they tried to make perfect stars and umbrellas. All you really need is sugar, a tiny pinch of baking soda, a small ladle, and a flat press (which can be a small plate or even the bottom of a mug if you're improvising). The trick is getting the heat just right – too hot and it burns, too cool and it won’t get that airy, brittle texture. It’s harder than it looks, and that's exactly why it became such a phenomenon. You can buy ready-made kits at larger marts or online, or simply gather the ingredients yourself.

Point: Making it yourself is the most authentic and fun way to engage with the dalgona challenge, especially with friends.

Dalgona's Lingering Legacy in Korean Pop Culture

Even if the daily dalgona candy craze has faded, its presence in Korean pop culture, especially among foreigners, remains. It’s become a recognizable symbol of Korea, a tangible piece of the hallyu (한류, Korean Wave) that Squid Game amplified globally. I still hear foreigners talking about it when they visit, linking it directly to their favorite K-drama. It’s fascinating how a simple street snack, originally called ppoppop by my grandparents, became a global icon. It's a testament to the power of media. So while you might not see Koreans lining up for it every day, the cultural footprint is deep. It's a reminder of a moment when the world looked at Korea, and it offered a sweet, albeit challenging, taste of our culture.

Point: Dalgona candy is now a global cultural icon, more than just a passing snack trend in Korea itself.

    Step 1: Gather Ingredients & Tools
    You'll need sugar, a tiny pinch of baking soda, a small metal ladle, a flat metal press, and a cookie cutter (for the shape).
  2. 2
    Step 2: Melt the Sugar
    Heat sugar in the ladle over a low flame, stirring constantly until it melts into a clear, golden syrup (don't burn it!).
  3. 3
    Step 3: Add Baking Soda
    Remove from heat, add a tiny pinch of baking soda, and stir vigorously until it foams up and turns light brown.
  4. 4
    Step 4: Press and Shape
    Pour the mixture onto a non-stick surface, let it cool for a few seconds, then press it flat and use your cookie cutter to make an imprint.
  5. 5
    Step 5: The Challenge
    Once cooled and hardened, use a toothpick to carefully cut out the imprinted shape without breaking the surrounding candy.

Quick Q&A

Q. Is dalgona candy still popular in Korea in 2026?

A. No, not as a widespread daily trend among locals. While it saw immense popularity during *Squid Game*'s initial release, it's now more of a nostalgic item for Koreans and a popular curiosity for foreign tourists.

Q. Where can tourists buy dalgona candy in Seoul?

A. Tourists can primarily find dalgona candy from street vendors in major tourist areas like Myeongdong, Insadong, and some traditional markets. Some cafes also offer dalgona-flavored drinks or desserts.

Q. What is the original name of dalgona candy in Korea?

A. The candy is traditionally known as ppoppop (뽑뽑) among older Koreans, though 'dalgona' has become the more widely recognized name due to its popularization.

Q. Can I make dalgona candy at home?

A. Yes, absolutely! Making your own dalgona is a popular activity. You can buy pre-made DIY kits at large supermarkets (like E-Mart or Lotte Mart) or simply use sugar, baking soda, a ladle, and a press.

Q. How much does dalgona candy cost in Seoul?

A. From a street vendor, a piece of dalgona typically costs between 2,000 to 5,000 won (approximately $1.50-$4 USD), depending on its size and where you purchase it.

달고나 & 오징어 게임: 서울에서 어디서 살 수 있나 (2026)

여러분은 아마 달고나 사탕(달고나)에 대한 온라인상의 화제를 보셨을 겁니다. 특히 *오징어 게임*이 폭발적인 인기를 얻은 후에요. 지금, 2026년 8월 현재 서울에서 달고나 사탕을 어디서 살 수 있는지 궁금해하는 외국인들을 위한 짧은 답변은 다음과 같습니다: 주변에 있지만, 예전만큼의 현상은 아닙니다. 요즘은 모든 한국인이 줄을 서서 먹는 것보다는 향수를 불러일으키는 간식이나 관광객 체험에 가깝습니다.

## 달고나 사탕은 (2026년 현재) 여전히 한국에서 큰 유행인가요?

솔직히 말해서, *오징어 게임*의 절정기 때처럼은 아닙니다. 쇼가 처음 방영되었을 때, 달고나(설탕으로 만든 바삭한 사탕으로, 원래 길거리 음식 형태로는 뽑뽑이라고도 불림)는 어디에나 있었습니다. 길거리 노점상들이 밤새 생겨났고, 카페들은 달고나 라떼를 출시했으며, 사람들은 이쑤시개로 모양을 잘라내려고 열렬히 노력했습니다. 그것은 진정한 열풍이었습니다. 이제 2026년에는 초기 열기가 현지인들 사이에서 확실히 식었습니다. 마치 계절 히트곡처럼 되었습니다. 모두가 알았고, 한동안 좋아했으며, 이제는 가끔 레트로 플레이리스트에서 나옵니다. 제 사무실에서는 누군가가 여전히 가끔 달고나 맛 스낵을 가져오는데, 보통 웃거나 추억을 되새기기 위해서이지, 더 이상 아무도 실제 챌린지를 하지는 않습니다. 주로 한국인에게는 향수를 불러일으키는 품목이고, 여전히 쇼와 연결시키는 관광객에게는 호기심의 대상입니다.

> 요점: 재미있는 기념품이나 달콤한 추억 여행이지, 현재 가장 뜨거운 것은 아닙니다.

## 길거리 노점상 및 전통 시장에서 달고나 사탕을 구매하는 곳

진정한 길거리 달고나 사탕 오징어 게임 경험을 찾고 있다면, 가장 좋은 구매처는 여전히 주요 관광 허브입니다. 명동(명동), 인사동(인사동), 홍대(홍대) 일부 지역에는 여전히 몇몇 전용 길거리 노점상들이 있습니다. 이 노점상들은 종종 휴대용 버너, 국자, 프레스, 다양한 모양 등 모든 장비를 갖추고 있습니다. 그들은 보통 사진 촬영 기회까지 제공하며 특히 관광객들을 대상으로 합니다. 최근 늦은 회식(퇴근 후 회사 저녁 식사) 후에 명동을 걷다가 거의 자정이었는데도 외국인 방문객들이 신나게 모양을 고르려고 줄 서 있는 것을 본 기억이 납니다. 길거리 노점상에서 달고나 한 조각의 가격은 일반적으로 크기와 모양의 복잡성에 따라 2,000원에서 5,000원(약 1.50달러~4달러) 정도입니다. 광장시장(광장시장)과 같은 대형 전통 시장에서도 한두 명의 노점상을 찾을 수 있지만, 절정기 때보다는 흔하지 않습니다.

> 요점: 관광 명소가 고전적인 길거리 노점상 경험을 위한 최고의 장소이지만, 약간 더 높은 가격을 예상하세요.

## 현대적인 달고나 변형: 카페, 편의점, 기념품

길거리 외에도 달고나는 현대 한국 간식 풍경에 더 미묘한 방식으로 통합되었습니다. 많은 카페에서는 여전히 달고나 라떼나 달고나 맛 디저트를 제공하는데, 여기서는 바삭하고 탄 설탕 맛이 음료나 토핑에 통합되어 있으며, 깨뜨려 먹는 단독 사탕은 아닙니다. 이것들은 꽤 흔하며 챌린지의 압박 없이 맛을 즐길 수 있는 좋은 방법이 될 수 있습니다. 제가 처음 달고나 라떼를 마셨을 때, 쌉쌀하고 달콤한 바삭함이 커피와 얼마나 잘 어울리는지 놀랐습니다. 편의점에서 달고나 사탕을 어디서 살 수 있는지 궁금해하는 분들을 위해, GS25나 CU와 같은 일부 대형 편의점(편의점)에서는 특히 인기 있는 계절이나 한정판 품목으로 미리 포장된 달고나 맛 스낵이나 실제 작은 사탕 조각을 가끔 재고로 둡니다. 일 년 내내 어디에서나 찾을 수는 없지만, 가끔 나타납니다. 또한, 이마트나 롯데마트와 같은 대형 마트(마트)나 관광 지역의 기념품 가게에서 기념품 스타일의 달고나 키트를 찾을 수 있습니다. 이 키트에는 일반적으로 작은 국자, 프레스, 특정 금속 모양이 포함되어 있어 집에서 직접 만들어 볼 수 있습니다.

> 요점: 카페는 번거로움 없이 맛을 제공하고, 키트는 DIY 재미에 좋으며, 편의점은 미리 만들어진 사탕을 찾기에는 복불복입니다.

## 나만의 달고나 만들기: 진정한 오징어 게임 챌린지

많은 사람들에게 달고나 사탕의 진정한 재미는, 특히 *오징어 게임*의 맥락에서, 단순히 먹는 것이 아니라 부러뜨리지 않고 모양을 조각해내는 것입니다. 여기서 직접 만드는 것이 중요합니다. 솔직히 말해서, 이것이 아마도 지금 그것을 경험하는 가장 보람 있는 방법일 것입니다. 쇼의 챌린지를 진정으로 생생하게 만들기 때문입니다. 제 동료가 최근에 아이를 위해 DIY 키트를 샀는데, 그들은 완벽한 별과 우산을 만들려고 노력하면서 온 토요일 오후를 웃고 소리 지르며 보냈습니다. 실제로 필요한 것은 설탕, 아주 작은 베이킹 소다 한 꼬집, 작은 국자, 그리고 평평한 프레스(작은 접시나 심지어 머그잔 바닥도 즉흥적으로 사용할 수 있습니다)뿐입니다. 비결은 열을 정확히 맞추는 것입니다. 너무 뜨거우면 타고, 너무 차가우면 그 공기 같고 바삭한 질감을 얻을 수 없습니다. 보기보다 어렵고, 바로 그것이 그렇게 큰 현상이 된 이유입니다. 대형 마트나 온라인에서 미리 만들어진 키트를 구매하거나, 단순히 재료를 직접 모을 수 있습니다.

> 요점: 직접 만드는 것이 달고나 챌린지를 가장 진정성 있고 재미있게 즐기는 방법이며, 특히 친구들과 함께 할 때 좋습니다.

## 한국 대중문화 속 달고나의 지속적인 유산

매일의 달고나 사탕 열풍이 식었더라도, 특히 외국인들 사이에서 한국 대중문화 속에서의 그 존재감은 여전히 남아 있습니다. 그것은 한국의 인식 가능한 상징이 되었고, *오징어 게임*이 전 세계적으로 증폭시킨 *한류*(한류, Korean Wave)의 실질적인 조각이 되었습니다. 저는 여전히 외국인들이 방문할 때 그것에 대해 이야기하고, 좋아하는 K-드라마와 직접 연결시키는 것을 듣습니다. 제 할아버지 할머니가 뽑뽑이라고 불렀던 단순한 길거리 간식이 어떻게 세계적인 아이콘이 되었는지 놀랍습니다. 그것은 미디어의 힘을 증명하는 것입니다. 그래서 한국인들이 매일 그것을 사기 위해 줄 서 있는 것을 보지 못할 수도 있지만, 문화적 발자취는 깊습니다. 그것은 세상이 한국을 바라보았고, 우리의 문화에 대한 달콤하지만 도전적인 맛을 제공했던 순간을 상기시켜 줍니다.

> 요점: 달고나 사탕은 이제 한국 자체의 일시적인 간식 트렌드를 넘어선 세계적인 문화 아이콘입니다.

It’s primarily a nostalgic item for Koreans, and a curiosity for tourists still connecting it to the show.

> Point: It's a fun memento or a sweet trip down memory lane, not the current hottest thing.

## Where to Buy Dalgona Candy from Street Vendors & Traditional Markets

If you're looking for that authentic, street-side dalgona candy Squid Game experience, your best bet for where to buy it is still in the major tourist hubs. Areas like Myeongdong (명동), Insadong (인사동), and parts of Hongdae (홍대) still have a handful of dedicated street vendors. These vendors often have the full setup: the portable burner, the ladle, the presses, and the array of shapes. They’re usually catering specifically to tourists, complete with photo opportunities. I remember walking through Myeongdong recently after a late hoesik (the after-work company dinner) and seeing a line of foreign visitors excitedly trying to choose their shape, even though it was almost midnight. The price for a piece of dalgona from a street vendor typically ranges from 2,000 to 5,000 won (roughly $1.50-$4 USD), depending on the size and complexity of the shape. You might also find a vendor or two in larger traditional markets, like Gwangjang Market (광장시장), though they're less common than during the peak.

> Point: Tourist hotspots are your best bet for the classic street vendor experience, but be prepared for a slightly higher price.

## Modern Dalgona Twists: Cafes, Convenience Stores, and Souvenirs

Beyond the street, dalgona has integrated itself into the modern Korean snack landscape in more subtle ways. Many cafes still offer dalgona lattes or dalgona-flavored desserts, where the crunchy, burnt-sugar flavor is incorporated into a drink or topping, rather than being a standalone candy you break. These are pretty common and can be a nice way to enjoy the taste without the pressure of the challenge. The first time I tried a dalgona latte, I was surprised by how well the bitter-sweet crunch complemented the coffee. For those wondering where to buy dalgona candy for convenience, some larger convenience stores (편의점, pyeon-ui-jeom) like GS25 or CU occasionally stock pre-packaged dalgona-flavored snacks or actual small pieces of the candy, especially around popular seasons or as a limited-edition item. You won't find it year-round everywhere, but it pops up. Additionally, you can find souvenir-style dalgona kits in large supermarkets (마트, mateu) like E-Mart or Lotte Mart, or in souvenir shops in tourist areas. These kits typically include the small ladle, a press, and the specific metal shapes, allowing you to try making it yourself at home.

> Point: Cafes offer the flavor without the fuss; kits are great for DIY fun; convenience stores are hit-or-miss for pre-made candy.

## Making Your Own Dalgona: The True Squid Game Challenge

For many, the real fun of dalgona candy, especially in the context of Squid Game, isn't just eating it but trying to carve out the shape without it breaking. This is where making your own comes in. Honestly, this is probably the most rewarding way to experience it now, as it truly brings the show's challenge to life. My coworker recently bought a DIY kit for his kid, and they spent an entire Saturday afternoon laughing and screaming as they tried to make perfect stars and umbrellas. All you really need is sugar, a tiny pinch of baking soda, a small ladle, and a flat press (which can be a small plate or even the bottom of a mug if you're improvising). The trick is getting the heat just right – too hot and it burns, too cool and it won’t get that airy, brittle texture. It’s harder than it looks, and that's exactly why it became such a phenomenon. You can buy ready-made kits at larger marts or online, or simply gather the ingredients yourself.

> Point: Making it yourself is the most authentic and fun way to engage with the dalgona challenge, especially with friends.

## Dalgona's Lingering Legacy in Korean Pop Culture

Even if the daily dalgona candy craze has faded, its presence in Korean pop culture, especially among foreigners, remains. It’s become a recognizable symbol of Korea, a tangible piece of the hallyu (한류, Korean Wave) that Squid Game amplified globally. I still hear foreigners talking about it when they visit, linking it directly to their favorite K-drama. It’s fascinating how a simple street snack, originally called ppoppop by my grandparents, became a global icon. It's a testament to the power of media. So while you might not see Koreans lining up for it every day, the cultural footprint is deep. It's a reminder of a moment when the world looked at Korea, and it offered a sweet, albeit challenging, taste of our culture.

> Point: Dalgona candy is now a global cultural icon, more than just a passing snack trend in Korea itself.

step.text: Heat sugar in the ladle over a low flame, stirring constantly until it melts into a clear, golden syrup (don't burn it!).

step.text: Pour the mixture onto a non-stick surface, let it cool for a few seconds, then press it flat and use your cookie cutter to make an imprint.
